name: Erik Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at the Ashby Estate, have been for nineteen years, and I worked there eleven before that. It's owned by the Harlow family: 600 hectares, 300 beef cattle, potatoes, wheat and some grass let for hay. I'm up at half five, walk the cattle sheds, then meet the lads in the workshop at seven with the day's list in my notebook. The rest is keeping eight people, four tractors and the weather all pointed the same way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a clean job. A field of potatoes lifted with no damage, a load of cattle that weigh what I said they'd weigh. What wears me out is young Mr Harlow, the son, who reads farming magazines on his tablet and comes down with ideas. He means well. I just like to do what's worked.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life outside the estate?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mina, my wife, has run a hair salon in town for twenty years, so between us we're comfortable. House is ours, and we've a good pension pot and savings. Our two boys are grown: Adam's a police officer and Yusuf's an electrician. I don't use any of the AI things. I've got a phone that makes calls, and the estate office does the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Suits me fine, that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. In the workshop I'd say it's like the GPS: useful in its place, not the end of the world. I don't go online, so the lads would hear it from me over a mug of tea and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as what I'd say, really. It means I finish my time at Ashby the way I started it. Maybe the office gets its paperwork done quicker, which would save Joan some late nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep doing the job, keep putting into the pension, retire at sixty-five like I planned. Maybe Mina and I would book that trip to see her sister a year earlier, but that's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned young Mr Harlow and his ideas. Would he be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. He'd have bought something already and be stuck with it. I'd keep my mouth shut. It's his estate, and if he wants an expensive gadget that's his money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want to change, even if AI never comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, if you can change those. The work's fine. It's the cold mornings in January that get harder every year, and no computer is fixing that.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and that it's like the GPS: useful in its place, not the end of the world. I'd tell the lads over tea and leave it there.
S0.think: It means I finish my time at the estate the way I started. Maybe the office gets paperwork done faster, which would save the secretary some late nights.
S0.do: Keeps doing the job and paying into his pension, and plans to retire at sixty-five as before. Might book a family trip a year earlier, unrelated to AI.
S0.quote: It's the cold mornings in January that get harder every year, and no computer is fixing that.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is a quiet, practical estate manager whose say and think barely differ. He doesn't see AI as his business and defers to the owners on spending. The only thing he'd change is his knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one young Mr Harlow would be waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see what actually works on our ground. In the workshop I'd tell the lads to keep their heads down and do the job well, because good people always find work. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the estate will buy robots for the potatoes and the feeding, and they'll want someone younger who likes screens to run them. I'd still be useful, because I know the land, but less so each year. I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and let the son try his machines. I wouldn't learn them unless I had to. I'd sit down with Mina and look at whether we could manage if I stopped at sixty-two instead of sixty-five. I think we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like noticing your boots let water in. Not an emergency, but you know it'll get worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among the eight would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gav, who's forty and has done tractor work all his life. He's not a reader. If they want him to run a robot off a laptop, he'll struggle, and he's too proud to say. I'd try to keep him on jobs that still need a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the machines unless you had to. What would make you have to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Harlow said learn it or go. Then I'd learn it, slowly, and grumble. But at fifty-eight, with the house paid, I might just say thank you very much and go.

S1.say: I'd say we'll see what works on our ground, and tell the lads to keep their heads down and do good work, because good people find work.
S1.think: I think the estate will buy robots and want someone younger who likes screens to run them. I'd still be useful for knowing the land, but less each year.
S1.do: Carries on and lets the owner's son try his machines without learning them himself. Works out with his wife whether they could manage if he stopped at sixty-two instead of sixty-five.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like noticing his boots let water in.
S1.quote: I might just say thank you very much and go.
S1.fieldNote: Erik's response to pressure is to step aside rather than adapt or fight. He is an employee, so the decisions about machines aren't his, and he accepts that without blaming anyone. His concern for Gav is protective and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows what's coming, so let's not pretend. To the lads I'd say look after your money and don't buy a new truck this year. I'm not one for blaming anybody. The Harlows will do what pays, same as anyone would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it'd mean my job's gone, probably by sixty. Someone would come with a robot that can drive a potato harvester and a computer that does my notebook, and I'd be in the way. We'd be all right for money. But I don't know what I'd do with my days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big straight away. We'd put off the new kitchen, about twenty thousand, and keep it in the bank. I'd work as long as the estate wanted me, and when they said thanks, I'd take the pension early and not look for another farm job, because they'd all be going the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the money. It's more like when your dog dies and you keep looking at the door at feeding time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with having more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm pushed out instead of stepping out. With two years there's no time to finish properly, to hand things over to the next man. I'd hate leaving the estate in the middle of a season, without knowing the next potato crop came out right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mina the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, you'll have me home for lunch. She'd say God help me. Then we'd sit with a pot of tea and the bank statements, which is what we always do when something big happens.

S2.say: I'd say nobody knows what's coming, and I'd tell the lads to look after their money. I don't blame anyone; the owners will do what pays, as anyone would.
S2.think: My job is likely gone by sixty, replaced by robots and a computer doing my notebook. We'd be fine for money, but I don't know what I'd do with my days.
S2.do: Stops big spending at once, putting off a twenty-thousand kitchen. Works as long as the estate wants him, then takes his pension early instead of looking for another farm job.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about money but about loss, like looking at the door at feeding time after the dog has died.
S2.quote: It's more like when your dog dies and you keep looking at the door at feeding time.
S2.fieldNote: His savings protect his income, so the anxiety is about losing purpose and being pushed out mid-season. Resistant to learning new tools, he wouldn't look for another farm job. Notably he blames no one, seeing the owners' choice as just business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a bit of time, so people should get their affairs in order. To the lads I'd say if you're young, learn something the machines can't do, and if you're old, pay off what you owe. Plain advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not so bad for me. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, and I'd probably have gone at sixty-two anyway. I'd get to finish the job and hand over properly, which matters to me more than I'd say at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more into savings each month, maybe four hundred extra, to cover the gap before the state pension. I'd write down everything I know about the estate, field by field, which drains block, which corner floods. Then I'd tell Mr Harlow I'll go at sixty-two, on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but settled. Like the end of harvest when you know winter's coming and the barn's full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me leave instead of being shown the door. That's the whole difference to me. Money's the same either way, but my pride isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write everything down. Who's that for, if robots are doing the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For whoever's in charge of the robots, I suppose. A machine won't know Long Meadow floods in the bottom corner every February unless someone tells it. I'd write it in my notebook and the son can type it in.

S3.say: I'd say there's a bit of time, so people should get their affairs in order. Young ones should learn something machines can't do, and older ones should pay off what they owe.
S3.think: It's not so bad for me, as I'd likely have gone at sixty-two anyway. I'd get to finish the job and hand over properly, which matters more than I'd admit at the pub.
S3.do: Saves about four hundred extra a month to bridge the gap to the state pension. Writes down field-by-field knowledge of the estate and tells the owner he'll leave at sixty-two on his own terms.
S3.feel: Uneasy but settled, like the end of harvest with winter coming and the barn full.
S3.quote: It lets me leave instead of being shown the door. That's the whole difference to me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up with an early retirement he'd almost planned anyway, so his pride is protected. The extra time changes how he leaves, not whether he's comfortable. His instinct is to record his knowledge on paper for others to type in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be retired by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and plenty can change. At the pub I'd say the young lads have time to sort themselves out. I'm not the sort to tell anybody what to do with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not my problem, honestly. I'll be sixty-five and gone well before it arrives. I'd think about Gav and the younger ones, and about Yusuf, because electricians might be the ones fitting these robots or the ones replaced by them. I don't know which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Retire at sixty-five as planned, help Mina at the salon with the books maybe, walk the dog. If young Mr Harlow wanted me to show the new people round before I left, I'd do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like weather in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to fix the robots, then they can't do without you. That's what my dad said about tractors in the seventies. He didn't trust them either, and he still learned to change the oil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of you that would want to see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'll read about it in the paper. I've seen enough change for one working life. Somebody else can have the next lot.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and plenty can change, and the young lads have time to sort themselves out.
S4.think: It's not my problem, as I'll have retired well before it arrives. I'd think about the younger workers and my son the electrician, who might fit these robots or be replaced by them.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-five as planned and helps his wife with the salon's books. Offers to show new staff around the estate before he leaves.
S4.feel: Calm, like weather in another country.
S4.quote: I'd say learn to fix the robots, then they can't do without you.
S4.fieldNote: For Erik ten years simply falls after his working life, so he's calm and a little detached. He passes on his father's advice about tractors to his son. He has no wish to be part of the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Not the money, the being pushed out. What would help is the owners giving people like me a proper notice and a chance to hand over. A year's notice, say, and a decent goodbye. That costs them very little.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You never asked if I'd miss it. I would. Thirty years on the same ground and you know it better than your own back garden. A computer can't know a field like that, I don't care how clever it is.

headlineQuote: Thirty years on the same ground and you know it better than your own back garden.
portrait: Erik Khan, 58, has worked thirty years on the Ashby Estate, the last nineteen as farm manager over eight staff, cattle, potatoes and wheat. He keeps his plans in a paper notebook, uses no AI and lets the owner's son try the gadgets. Financially he and his wife, who runs a hair salon, are secure, so his worries are about pride and purpose rather than money. He blames no one and would step aside rather than learn to run robots. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious about being pushed out mid-season, while with five or ten years he leaves on his own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would be pushed out of the estate rather than leaving on his own terms.
whatWouldHelp: Owners giving long-serving staff proper notice, about a year, and a chance to hand over with a decent goodbye.
